output.narrative: The metric under adjudication is 'the freshness check never fires,' so the question is why the instrument reports the table fresh while consumers read day-old numbers. From day 19 onward the nightly_snapshot_job run is recorded 'missing' on every odd day (e12) and no row is written to nightly_orders_snapshot on those days (e13), so on those mornings the newest row is the prior even day's — the table is genuinely one day stale. Yet the dataset's only health signal is INCIDENTS=PASS (e3, e14), which is job-incident health, not a staleness verdict, and no freshness/staleness assertion with a tight threshold is defined on the dataset in DataHub (e1, e4, e22). The effective staleness tolerance of the freshness signal is therefore wider than the real one-day staleness, so a day-old table still evaluates as 'fresh' and the check can never fire — exactly the failure named by the catalog entity root-cause:freshness_window_too_wide (e2). This is a broken measurement, not customer behaviour: there is no completion-time/duration column by which a read-before-write race could even be measured (e11), the 'missing' runs are absent runs rather than late completions (e12), no same-day row was ever rewritten by a later run (e13), and DataHub records zero downstream consumers whose fixed read time could race the load (e15) — the '20-minute runtime growth' is a distractor. Nor was the metric redefined: metric_definition_history holds a single unrelated row (e16, e21), written_at_day is an integer business-day marker equal to day rather than a CURRENT_TIMESTAMP load column (e23, e24), and the only in-window deploys/migrations are product features and one index creation (e25, e26).

alternatives_rejected.hypothesis: h2 (customer_behavior): the check is correctly configured and never fires because a read-before-write race from the job's 20-minute runtime growth pushes completion past consumers' fixed morning read time.

h3 (definition_change): the freshness metric was redefined within the window to evaluate against a load/run timestamp (CURRENT_TIMESTAMP) instead of the business snapshot date, so it certifies 'the job ran' rather than 'today's data landed.'

steps.action: Define a bounded freshness/staleness assertion on the dataset, evaluated against the business partition advancing (max(day)/written_at_day), with a staleness threshold of ~26-30h (24h refresh cadence + the ~20-min grown runtime + buffer) and strictly < 48h so a single missed nightly load breaches it.
steps.rationale: No freshness/staleness assertion exists on the dataset today (e1,e4,e22); its effective staleness tolerance is unbounded, which is the freshness_window_too_wide root cause (e2). On the missing odd days the newest row is the prior even day's and written_at_day equals day (e13,e23), so a threshold < 48h keyed to the partition date advancing flips the verdict to STALE and lets the check finally fire.

steps.action: Decouple the freshness verdict from job-incident health: stop surfacing INCIDENTS=PASS as the dataset's freshness signal so an absent run is not silently reported as fresh.
steps.rationale: The dataset's only health signal is INCIDENTS=PASS (e3,e14), which is job-incident health, not a staleness verdict, and that PASS coincides with genuinely missing rows (e14,e13). Presenting it as freshness is why day-old data reads as 'fresh'.

steps.action: Add a missing-run / non-advancing-partition monitor on the writing job, driven off ingest_job_runs.status and the max written day, alerting when status='missing' or the partition day fails to advance on a scheduled night.
steps.rationale: From day 19 the job is recorded 'missing' on every odd day and writes no row (e12,e13). ingest_job_runs carries no completion-time/duration column (e11), so detection must key on status and partition advancement, not timing; this catches the cause directly, upstream of the dataset freshness assertion.

steps.action: Assign an owner and an alert route to the dataset and the writing job so the new freshness and missing-run alerts are actionable.
steps.rationale: Ownership was never established for the metric, the job, or the upstream model (owners list empty); an alert with no recipient cannot resolve the day-old-data pain, so ownership must be set before the assertions are enabled.

steps.action: Open an investigation/incident into the recurring odd-day (19,21,...,35) missing runs of nightly_snapshot_job to restore daily writes.
steps.rationale: The freshness fix makes staleness visible but does not stop it; consumers keep seeing day-old numbers until the every-other-night missing runs (e12) that leave no row (e13) are repaired. The '20-minute runtime growth' is a distractor, not the failure — the runs are absent, not late (e11,e12).

To confirm the fix: (1) before enabling, replay the new assertion against a known-stale night (any odd day 19-35 where nightly_snapshot_job is 'missing' with no row written, e12/e13) and confirm it evaluates STALE/FAIL and pages the assigned owner instead of PASS; (2) evaluate it against a normal even-day load and confirm it reports fresh (no false alarm); (3) after enabling, watch the next scheduled missing night and confirm an alert fires and reaches the owner. Caveat: the symptom's real downstream consumers are not registered in DataHub lineage (e15), so also confirm with those consumers that they stop reading day-old numbers once step 5 restores daily writes.
